content: Approximately 5 billion years ago, the age of the Earth is defined chronometrically rather than stratigraphically. By 8 billion years ago, at the end of the Hadean eon, significant geological and planetary changes had occurred. At the beginning of the Archean eon, Earth's heat flow was nearly three times higher than it is today. By the start of the Proterozoic eon, it was still twice the current level. This excess heat likely originated from residual heat from planetary accretion, the formation of the iron core, and radiogenic heat production from short-lived radionuclides such as uranium-235. Volcanic activity during this time was significantly higher than today, with numerous hotspots, rift valleys, and eruptions of unusual lavas like komatiite. Intrusive igneous rocks, including large melt sheets, extensive plutonic masses of granite, diorite, ultramafic to mafic layered intrusions, anorthosites, and sanukitoids, were prevalent in the crystalline cratonic remnants of the Archean crust that still exist today. The tectonic style of early Archean Earth may have been different from the modern era. Some scientists propose that the hotter Earth led to more vigorous plate tectonic activity, resulting in a higher rate of crustal recycling. This may have delayed the formation of stable cratons and continents until the mantle cooled and convection slowed. Others argue that the subcontinental lithospheric mantle was too buoyant to subduct and that the scarcity of Archean rocks is due to erosion from subsequent tectonic events. The existence of plate tectonic activity during the Archean remains a topic of active geoscientific research. Large continents did not form until late in the Archean. Instead, small protocontinents were the norm, prevented from coalescing into larger landmasses by the high rate of geological activity. These felsic protocontinents likely formed at hotspots rather than subduction zones, originating from processes such as the igneous differentiation of mafic rocks, partial melting of mafic magma, granitization of intermediate rocks, and metamorphic alteration of felsic sedimentary rocks. Continental fragments that were not buoyant enough or fortunate enough to avoid subduction zones may not have been preserved. Another explanation for the lack of early Archean rocks older than 3.8 billion years is the presence of significant extrasolar debris in the early solar system. Even after planetary formation, large volumes of asteroids and meteorites bombarded the early Earth until approximately 3.8 billion years ago. The late heavy bombardment, a period of intense impacts, may have shattered early protocontinents, preventing the formation of large crustal fragments. The Archean atmosphere lacked free oxygen. Despite this, temperatures were near modern levels within 500 million years of Earth's formation, as evidenced by the presence of sedimentary rocks within highly deformed gneisses. Astronomers believe the Sun was about one-third dimmer during this time, which may have contributed to lower global temperatures. However, larger amounts of greenhouse gases likely compensated for the reduced solar output. By the end of the Archean, around 2.6 billion years ago, plate tectonic activity may have resembled modern Earth, as evidenced by well-preserved sedimentary basins, volcanic arcs, intracontinental rifts, continent-continent collisions, and widespread orogenic events. These suggest the assembly and destruction of one or more supercontinents. Liquid water was abundant, and deep oceanic basins existed, as indicated by banded iron formations, chert beds, chemical sediments, and pillow basalts. The oldest rock formations exposed on Earth's surface are Archean or slightly older, although a few mineral grains predate this period. Archean rocks are found in regions such as Greenland, the Canadian Shield, the Baltic Shield, Scotland, India, Brazil, western Australia, and southern Africa. While the first continents formed during this eon, Archean rocks account for only 7% of the world's current cratons. Even considering erosion and destruction of past formations, evidence suggests that only 5-40% of the present continental crust formed during the Archean. Archean rocks are often heavily metamorphosed deep-water sediments, such as graywackes, mudstones, volcanic sediments, and banded iron formations. Carbonate rocks are rare, indicating that the oceans were more acidic due to dissolved carbon dioxide compared to the Proterozoic. Greenstone belts, typical Archean formations, consist of alternating highand low-grade metamorphic rocks. The high-grade rocks originated from volcanic island arcs, while the low-grade rocks represent deep-sea sediments eroded from neighboring island arcs and deposited in forearc basins. Greenstone belts represent sutured protocontinents. Fossils of cyanobacterial mats, known as stromatolites, are found throughout the Archean and become especially common late in the eon. Probable bacterial fossils have also been identified in chert beds. In addition to the domain Bacteria, microfossils of the extremophilic domain Archaea have been identified. Life likely existed throughout the Archean but was limited to simple, non-nucleated single-celled organisms called Prokaryota. There are no known eukaryotic fossils from this time, although eukaryotes may have evolved during the Archean without leaving fossil evidence. No fossil evidence exists for ultramicroscopic intracellular replicators such as viruses.
